title: The King's Experiment with Pleasure and Work
summary: The Teacher tests pleasure, wine, and great building projects, acquiring houses, vineyards, gardens, servants, flocks, treasure, singers, and concubines. He denies himself nothing, yet finds it all futile. He then weighs wisdom against folly and finds wisdom better, but both the wise and the fool die and are forgotten. He comes to hate his toil, since he must leave its fruit to someone else, and ends by recognizing that the simple ability to eat, drink, and enjoy work comes from the hand of God.
story: Chapter 1 announced the Teacher's search. Chapter 2 carries it out. Speaking in the voice of a king with unlimited means, he tries every path people take to find satisfaction: pleasure, achievement, wealth, and wisdom. Each is tested and each fails to give lasting gain, above all because of death. Yet at the chapter's end a new note sounds for the first time, one that will recur throughout the book: the ordinary goods of food, drink, and work are gifts from God, and apart from him no one can enjoy them. The chapter moves from grasping at everything to receiving something.
historical:
The Teacher's building projects recall Solomon's reign as described in 1 Kings 3 to 11: his palaces and the temple, his great wealth in silver and gold, his many servants, his horses and chariots, his wide-ranging trade, and his seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. The list in verses 4 to 8 reads like a royal boast, and the first readers would have heard in it the glory of Israel's greatest king.

Whether or not Solomon wrote the words, the chapter uses this royal persona to test life at its most privileged. If even the wealthiest and wisest king in Israel's memory found no lasting gain in all he built, no one else will. The word translated parks in verse 5 (pardes) is a loanword from Persian, one of the linguistic features many scholars cite in dating the book to the Persian period or later; the same word eventually gave English the word paradise.
cultural:
Royal gardens and parks were symbols of power in the ancient Near East. Assyrian and Persian kings planted vast parks stocked with trees and animals from across their empires, watered by canals and reservoirs, as displays of their dominion over nature. Reservoirs, like the ones mentioned in verse 6, were essential in a land with little rainfall and were major feats of engineering. Male and female singers performed at royal banquets, and a large harem was a sign of royal status and a way to cement alliances through marriage.

The Teacher's concern about who will inherit his work (verses 18 to 21) reflects the importance of inheritance in the ancient world. Family property and wealth were passed to sons, and a man's legacy was tied to what he left behind. Solomon's own son, Rehoboam, lost most of his father's kingdom through foolish decisions (1 Kings 12), a story that gives verse 19 a sharp edge for readers who knew it.
literary: The chapter is written as a first-person memoir, with many verbs in the first person: I built, I planted, I made, I acquired. The repetition of for myself in verses 4 to 8 underlines the self-focus of the experiment. The chapter has a clear arc: the experiment with pleasure and building (verses 1 to 11), the comparison of wisdom and folly (verses 12 to 17), the despair over leaving one's work to others (verses 18 to 23), and the turn to enjoyment as God's gift (verses 24 to 26). The refrains of chapter 1 continue: futile, a pursuit of the wind, and under the sun. The key verb shifts from I did to I hated and finally to I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.

outline.t: Great works, great wealth, and no gain
Wisdom and folly: one fate for both
Hating toil that must be left to another
Eating, drinking, and work as God's gift

doctrines.note: The Teacher's experiment shows what happens when good things like pleasure, work, and wealth are asked to supply ultimate meaning. They cannot bear that weight, and the one who pursues them for their own sake ends up hating life.
Verses 24 to 26 say that the ability to enjoy food and work comes from the hand of God. Enjoyment is not something we can produce by acquiring more; it is a gift God gives.
Death is the great leveler: the wise man dies like the fool (verse 16). The chapter raises the question of justice that the book will answer only at its end, with God's judgment of every deed.

words.note: Amal, toil or labor, often with a sense of trouble or weariness. It appears nine times in this chapter. It describes both the work itself and its fruit. In Ecclesiastes amal often carries the weight of Genesis 3, where the ground was cursed and work became painful.

Miqreh, fate or what happens. The word refers to what befalls a person, especially death, not to a blind fate independent of God. The Teacher's complaint is that the same miqreh overcomes both the wise and the fool (verse 14).

Pardes, park or garden. A Persian loanword, it described a walled royal park. The Greek translation of the Old Testament used a related word, paradeisos, for the garden of Eden, which is where English gets paradise. Here it is one of the king's great works that bring no lasting gain.

Simchah, joy or pleasure. The Teacher tests pleasure in verse 1 and finds it futile, yet in verse 26 God gives joy to the one who pleases him. The difference is between joy grasped as a goal and joy received as a gift.

christ: The Teacher discovers that even a king's wealth and wisdom cannot overcome death or secure a lasting legacy. Jesus' parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21), who builds bigger barns and dies that night, makes the same point: whose will these things be? Jesus also said that one greater than Solomon had come, and he taught that a person's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Where the Teacher's great works turn to despair, the New Testament promises that work done in the Lord is not in vain because of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:58). These connections are thematic: Ecclesiastes exposes the problem that the gospel addresses.

hard.q: Is the Teacher recommending that we eat, drink, and be merry because life is pointless?
hard.a: Verse 24 says nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. Out of context, this could sound like a resigned hedonism: since nothing lasts, enjoy what you can. Some interpreters read the Teacher's enjoyment passages this way, as a sad second-best in a futile world. But the verse goes on to say that this is from the hand of God, and verse 25 adds that apart from him no one can find enjoyment. Many interpreters therefore read these passages as the book's positive counsel: receive ordinary goods as God's gifts rather than trying to extract ultimate meaning from them. The difference from hedonism is that the enjoyment is received from God, not grasped as a substitute for him. The chapter's final verse still ends with futility, showing that even this answer does not resolve every question.

questions: The Teacher denied himself nothing and still found it futile. What do you tend to reach for when you want satisfaction, and what happens?
Verse 19 worries about who will inherit one's work. How does knowing you can't control your legacy change the way you work?
How is enjoying food and work as a gift from God different from pursuing pleasure for its own sake?
